title: Oscillations, waves and sound
note: Simple harmonic motion arises whenever the restoring force is proportional to displacement; its period does not depend on amplitude. A wave carries energy, not matter, and its speed is v = fλ, set by the medium. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave, about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C.

read.title: Back and forth
text: Pull a mass on a spring and let go: it oscillates because the spring always pulls it back toward equilibrium with a force proportional to the displacement. Motion driven by such a restoring force is simple harmonic motion. Its period, 2π√(m/k), does not depend on how far you pull it. A pendulum swinging through small angles behaves the same way, with a period 2π√(L/g) that ignores the mass of the bob.

A wave is an oscillation that travels. Shake one end of a rope and a pulse runs along it, yet each bit of rope only moves up and down; energy travels, matter stays. In a transverse wave the medium moves perpendicular to the wave's travel; in a longitudinal wave, such as sound, it moves back and forth along it. Every wave obeys v = fλ, and the speed is set by the medium, not by the source.

When two waves overlap, their displacements add. In phase they reinforce; out of phase they cancel. Waves reflecting back and forth on a guitar string interfere to form standing waves, and only wavelengths that fit the string's length survive. Those allowed frequencies give each instrument its notes.

q.q: What sets the speed of a wave?
What moves along a rope when a pulse travels down it?
Why does a guitar string sound only certain frequencies?
o: Only wavelengths fitting the string form standing waves
